summary: Authentication tokens, session identifiers, and identity attributes that are implicitly and automatically attached by the client runtime (browser or OS) to an outbound request based solely on the target destination, rather than being explicitly and deliberately attached by application logic for each distinct user action.

bounded_scope.covers: Browser-managed session cookies, cached HTTP Basic/Digest authentication, TLS client certificates, Kerberos/NTLM ambient tokens, and the architectural distinction between implicit environmental authority and explicit programmatic authorization.
bounded_scope.delegates: SameSite cookie scoping and browser default policies are delegated to concept.samesite-cookies; cross-origin dispatch boundaries are delegated to concept.same-origin-policy; token-based anti-CSRF synchronizer patterns are analyzed in topic.csrf.

learning_objectives: Distinguish ambient credentials (automatically appended by the runtime environment) from explicit credentials (programmatically supplied by application code).
Trace how the automatic attachment of ambient credentials transforms the browser into an unwitting confused deputy on behalf of untrusted origins.
mental_model: An ambient credential is like an automated electronic company badge pinned to a messenger's coat. Whenever the messenger approaches the corporate headquarters building, the gate sensor reads the badge and unlocks the doors—without checking whether the messenger was dispatched by the company CEO or tricked by a rival. Because the browser automatically attaches cookies to every request matching the target domain, the receiving server cannot determine whether the request was intentionally triggered by the user or surreptitiously provoked by a third-party website.
mechanism: When an HTTP request is dispatched from a browser context, the browser inspects its internal credential stores: (1) Cookie Jar: Any cookie matching the target domain and path (subject to SameSite and Secure attributes) is automatically formatted into a 'Cookie: ...' request header. (2) HTTP Authentication: If credentials were provided previously for the realm via HTTP Basic or Digest, the browser automatically injects the cached 'Authorization' header. (3) Client Certificates: If mutual TLS (mTLS) is established, the browser completes the TLS handshake using the local client certificate. (4) Operating System Authentication: On Windows/Active Directory, NTLM/Negotiate authentication headers are automatically negotiated. In all these cases, the user-agent attaches authority implicitly without requiring JavaScript on the originating page to know, handle, or explicitly approve the credential. When a malicious third-party origin induces the browser to issue an HTTP request (via HTML form submission, fetch, image tag, or script), the ambient credential attachment mechanism fires automatically unless explicit cross-site restrictions prevent it.
security_relevance: CSRF: The entire vulnerability class relies on ambient credentials (primarily session cookies) being attached to cross-site requests.
Confused Deputy Problem: The browser acts as an intermediary possessing authority (cookies) that an unauthorized caller (malicious web page) abuses to execute actions.
Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking (CSWSH): WebSocket handshakes automatically include ambient cookies, enabling unauthorized full-duplex socket establishment from malicious origins.

Authorization Architecture: Explains why Bearer tokens stored in non-ambient storage (e.g. in-memory JavaScript variables) require explicit attachment and are inherently immune to classic CSRF, but more vulnerable to XSS.

common_assumptions.assumption: If a request contains valid user session cookies, the user must have intentionally initiated the action.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: The browser attaches cookies automatically based on destination domain matching, irrespective of whether the request originated from the user's intent or an attacker's cross-site script.
common_assumptions.security_implication: State-changing operations without secondary, non-ambient verification (such as anti-CSRF tokens or SameSite=Strict cookies) are vulnerable to forgery.

common_assumptions.assumption: Setting HttpOnly on session cookies prevents CSRF.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: HttpOnly blocks JavaScript from reading document.cookie (defending against token theft via XSS). It does not stop the browser from automatically sending the cookie on HTTP requests across origins.
common_assumptions.security_implication: Developers believe HttpOnly protects against CSRF, leaving the application completely unprotected against cross-site requests.

common_assumptions.assumption: Requiring POST requests instead of GET prevents ambient credential abuse.
common_assumptions.why_wrong: HTML <form method='POST'> elements automatically submit cross-origin POST requests with full ambient cookies.
common_assumptions.security_implication: Relying on HTTP method switching as a security boundary fails against standard automated form submission payloads.

sources.title: RFC 6265 - HTTP State Management Mechanism
sources.claim: Specifies cookie storage and transmission rules, establishing that user agents automatically attach cookies matching domain and path to outbound HTTP requests.

sources.title: Hardy, Norm - The Confused Deputy (ACM Operating Systems Review)
sources.claim: Establishes the foundational concept of the confused deputy problem, wherein an entity with authority is tricked into using its authority for unauthorized purposes.

sources.title: PortSwigger - Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)
sources.claim: Explains that CSRF relies on the browser automatically including credentials (such as session cookies) with cross-origin requests.
